common_name: Maui Magic Elephant Ear (Vigorous Purple-Black Colocasia)

planting.note: Plant tubers 2-3 inches deep in warm, saturated soil after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed.

directions: Maui Magic is a robust, vigorous relative of the more common Black Magic elephant ear, producing large arrow-shaped leaves in deep purple-black on dark, upright stems. Grow in consistently moist to boggy, fertile soil with dappled sun to light shade; full Gulf Coast sun is tolerated only with heavy irrigation. Feed monthly through the growing season with a balanced fertilizer to sustain its larger stature, and divide congested clumps every two to three years to maintain vigor. In zone 8, dig and store tubers over winter or heavily mulch in place where the freeze line is shallow.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Jack's Giant Elephant Ear (Oversized Near-Black Colocasia)

planting.note: Give tubers extra room when planting after last frost, since this cultivar quickly outgrows typical elephant ear spacing.

directions: Jack's Giant is prized for exceptionally large, near-black leaves on thick dark petioles, forming a bold specimen clump that dwarfs standard black-leaf cultivars. Site in rich, constantly moist soil in partial shade to filtered sun, and allow generous spacing since mature clumps can reach imposing size in a single Gulf Coast growing season. Heavy monthly feeding and reliable irrigation are essential to reach full size; skimping on either produces a noticeably smaller plant. Overwinter tubers indoors in zone 8, or grow as a dramatic annual accent elsewhere.

common_name: Pineapple Princess Elephant Ear (Narrow Serrated Chartreuse Colocasia)

planting.note: Plant tubers after soil has warmed following last frost; brighter light than typical elephant ears intensifies its unusual leaf form and color.

directions: Pineapple Princess is an unusual, compact Colocasia selection with narrow, twisted, deeply serrated chartreuse-green leaves that resemble a pineapple crown rather than a typical broad elephant ear. Grow in moist, fertile soil with more direct sun than other Colocasia cultivars tolerate, which keeps the foliage compact and brightly colored rather than lax and green. Keep soil consistently damp, feed monthly, and use it as a textural container or border accent rather than a bold specimen plant. Lift and store tubers before frost in zone 8 or treat as a warm-season annual.

common_name: Distant Memory Elephant Ear (Glossy Near-Black Ruffled Colocasia)

planting.note: Plant tubers 2-3 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost; deep, wet soil produces the most vivid gloss on the near-black leaves.

directions: Distant Memory produces glossy, deeply ruffled leaves in an inky near-black shade that catches light dramatically along pond edges or in large containers. Plant in constantly moist to boggy, fertile soil in partial shade, since too much direct sun can dull the leaf sheen and scorch margins in peak Gulf Coast summer heat. Feed monthly through the growing season and keep soil saturated for the darkest color and best ruffling. Where winters dip below the low 20s, lift tubers and store dry and frost-free until spring.

common_name: Chicago Harlequin Elephant Ear (White-Splashed Variegated Colocasia)

planting.note: Plant tubers after last frost in bright, filtered light, which shows off the irregular cream-white variegation best.

directions: Chicago Harlequin is a striking sport of the purple-stemmed Fontanesii type, with green leaves irregularly streaked and splashed in creamy white, and it holds its variegation better than many patterned Colocasia in partial shade to filtered sun. Grow in rich, consistently moist soil, watching for any all-green reversion shoots and removing them promptly at the base to preserve the pattern. Feed lightly but regularly, since excess nitrogen can push plain green growth at the expense of variegation. Store tubers indoors over winter in zone 8 or grow as a striking annual foliage accent farther north.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Puckered Up Elephant Ear (Heavily Textured Dark Colocasia)

planting.note: Plant tubers in warm, moist soil after last frost; heavy irrigation intensifies the deeply puckered leaf texture.

directions: Puckered Up stands out for its heavily quilted, deeply textured dark green-to-purple leaf surface, which adds strong visual interest even without variegation or bright color. Plant in rich, evenly moist soil in partial shade, where the puckered texture shows to best effect without leaf scorch. Water deeply and often during hot weather, since consistent moisture is what produces the most pronounced surface texture. Divide crowded clumps every couple of years and overwinter tubers indoors in zone 8 or treat as an annual in cooler areas.

common_name: Compacta Shell Ginger (Dwarf Variegated Shell Ginger)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring after soil has warmed, in a lightly shaded bed or large container.

directions: Compacta is a dwarf form of shell ginger that stays under three feet tall, making it far easier to fit into foundation plantings and mixed containers than the standard 6-8 foot species. Grow in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun, protecting it from harsh afternoon exposure that can scorch the glossy foliage. Water regularly during the growing season and reduce watering somewhat in winter dormancy. In zone 8, the top growth typically dies back after a hard freeze but the rhizomes recover reliably from a deep protective mulch layer.

common_name: Jungle Queen Red Ginger (Soft Pink-Flowered Alpinia)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring once nighttime temperatures stay reliably warm, in a sheltered, humid spot.

directions: Jungle Queen is a soft-pink-bracted sport of the familiar scarlet Red Ginger, forming tall clumping canes topped with cone-shaped pink flower spikes prized for cutting. Grow in warm, humid, partially shaded conditions with rich, consistently moist soil, sheltered from drying wind that can brown the leaf tips. Feed monthly during the growing season to sustain strong cane production and repeat flowering. This cultivar has little cold tolerance, so in zone 9 protect the root zone heavily over winter or grow it in a large pot that can be moved under cover during cold snaps.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in a lightly shaded bed or border once soil has warmed.

directions: Alpinia formosana is a compact clumping ginger from Taiwan with narrow, strap-like leaves striped in cream and green, forming a neat low mound well suited to edging shaded beds. Grow in fertile, well-drained but consistently moist soil in partial shade, where the variegation stays crisp without leaf burn. It spreads slowly by rhizome to form a dense, well-behaved clump that rarely needs division more than every few years. In zone 8, foliage dies back after a hard freeze but the plant typically resprouts from the roots in spring given a good mulch layer.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring once temperatures are reliably warm, in humus-rich soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Costus malortieanus, sometimes called fuzzy spiral ginger, has soft, velvety, light green leaves banded with darker chevron markings arranged in the genus's signature spiral pattern along low, creeping stems. Grow in consistently moist, organically rich soil in partial to deep shade, since the fuzzy foliage scorches quickly in direct sun. It performs beautifully as a shaded groundcover or container specimen and produces small yellow flowers from a cone-like bract at the stem tip. In zone 9, mulch heavily over winter or grow it as a container plant that can be moved indoors before frost.

common_name: Snow Cap Costus (Orange Tulip Spiral Ginger)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring once soil has warmed, in a partly shaded spot with rich, moist soil.

directions: Snow Cap is a compact selection of Costus curvibracteatus grown for its cream-white bracts that set off small tubular orange flowers resembling tiny tulips, held above spiraling ranks of glossy green leaves. Plant in rich, evenly moist soil in partial shade to filtered sun, and keep humidity high for the best flowering display. Feed lightly during the growing season and cut spent flowering canes to the base once they decline to make room for fresh growth. In zone 9, protect the crown with heavy mulch over winter or overwinter divisions in containers indoors.
